Hiya, I live in London and currently work on a consumer app that's unrelated to all this.

However, lately I've been gripped by the idea that the way we build our computing systems today can't possibly be sustainable. Assuming we're still computing in 1000 years, I'm convinced it won't look like this—so how do we start moving in that direction?

At the beginning of my career almost 20 years ago I worked on a system at MAYA Design (Civium/Visage/VIA Repository) that used unconventional approaches like storing data in key-value dictionaries with UUIDs that could be easily distributed/synced across the network, as well as a message-based/boxes-and-wires programming model where the code modules were also stored in these dictionaries, so that computing could happen wherever was convenient. (It mostly worked, but was a bit slow.)

I'm interested in seeing what systems have been built since then that explore similar ideas, since I feel that data storage & management is a useful lens to help us see the future of computing. I've already spent a few days following links from this Slack, and the closest things I found so far were the Houyhnhnm Computing essays, Sandstorm.io, IPFS, Urbit, and Camlistore. (I'd appreciate pointers to other things in that vein.)

I'm also very interested in the meta-problem of how to architect new technologies in a way that aligns people's and companies' incentives to increase their chances of getting developed and adopted.

Thanks to @Steve Krouse for building this beacon to help us find each other, and to @Stefan Lesser for getting me on board. Looking forward to meeting some of you at a future London meetup!

#
Hi everyone! Lately I tend to introduce myself as a barbarian programmer. I mean that in a few different ways:

• I tend to be a curmudgeon, happier by myself than "organizing" into groups to achieve some shared goal. This doesn't mean I dislike collaboration. I just think we tend to conflate collaboration with synchronous collaboration, and asynchronous collaboration is a better fit for many tasks. Asynchronous collaboration can span great distances in space and time. You reading Aristotle could be asynchronous collaboration -- if you are then able to build on what you read in some way and put out some artifact that someone else can collaborate with. UX people like to say "don't make me think". I like to say "don't make me talk to you". Show me what you built in a form that I can read, listen to, play interactively with and gradually understand/appreciate. I may still come talk to you if the situation merits it (I actually love talking to people, believe it or not), but give me the choice.
• I think we've been doing city-living cheek-by-jowl for so long that we've forgotten what benefits it has, and continue cargo-culting it long after it's become superfluous. I don't mean that literally; I love living in cities. But our software stacks have many of the same patterns as cities, and they aren't really necessary: a) promiscuously adding dependencies, b) relying implicitly on some sort of division of labor, so that if we find a problem in a dependency we don't feel empowered to fix it for ourselves, instead turning to ways to try to get others to do it for us like paying, bullying, cajoling, passing laws, etc. It's worth swinging that pendulum back a bit, to imagine we're out on the steppe with just what we have on our backs and nobody else around for miles, and try to achieve our ends with 10x fewer libraries and frameworks. (More details: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=16882140#16882555 .)
• It emphasizes sustainability. When you live off the land (I gather; I wouldn't actually know) you are more attuned to how you affect your environment. Your externalities. We city dwellers just expect someone else to cart our trash out for us.

Unfortunately this is all aspirational, because the way we write software doesn't really work for a barbarian. I've been working very slowly on extricating a kernel of software and way of writing software that can be more self-sufficient and sustainable. author: Kartik Agaram
text:
Hi everyone! Lately I tend to introduce myself as a barbarian programmer. I mean that in a few different ways:

• I tend to be a curmudgeon, happier by myself than "organizing" into groups to achieve some shared goal. This doesn't mean I dislike collaboration. I just think we tend to conflate collaboration with synchronous collaboration, and asynchronous collaboration is a better fit for many tasks. Asynchronous collaboration can span great distances in space and time. You reading Aristotle could be asynchronous collaboration -- if you are then able to build on what you read in some way and put out some artifact that someone else can collaborate with. UX people like to say "don't make me think". I like to say "don't make me talk to you". Show me what you built in a form that I can read, listen to, play interactively with and gradually understand/appreciate. I may still come talk to you if the situation merits it (I actually love talking to people, believe it or not), but give me the choice.
• I think we've been doing city-living cheek-by-jowl for so long that we've forgotten what benefits it has, and continue cargo-culting it long after it's become superfluous. I don't mean that literally; I love living in cities. But our software stacks have many of the same patterns as cities, and they aren't really necessary: a) promiscuously adding dependencies, b) relying implicitly on some sort of division of labor, so that if we find a problem in a dependency we don't feel empowered to fix it for ourselves, instead turning to ways to try to get others to do it for us like paying, bullying, cajoling, passing laws, etc. It's worth swinging that pendulum back a bit, to imagine we're out on the steppe with just what we have on our backs and nobody else around for miles, and try to achieve our ends with 10x fewer libraries and frameworks. (More details: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=16882140#16882555 .)
• It emphasizes sustainability. When you live off the land (I gather; I wouldn't actually know) you are more attuned to how you affect your environment. Your externalities. We city dwellers just expect someone else to cart our trash out for us.

Unfortunately this is all aspirational, because the way we write software doesn't really work for a barbarian. I've been working very slowly on extricating a kernel of software and way of writing software that can be more self-sufficient and sustainable. Hello everyone! Many thanks to @Stefan Lesser for inviting me to this place. My name is Joel and I live in Cambridge, UK, where I completed my CS undergraduate degree last summer. For the past year I've been a software engineer in a local startup. But it is my working on my blog (https://programmingmadecomplicated.wordpress.com) and on the general vision that we share here, that gives me true fulfillment - especially since nobody I've met in real life expresses any sort of interest or enthusiasm about this sort of thing. Fortunately I've found many who do online, and I'll eagerly attend any meetups in the UK.

Origin story is, in a nutshell: I wanted to make games as a kid so I learned GameMaker. I then traded the ability to make games for learning to Code Properly and now I want my creativity-outlet back :angry:

I would try different programming languages and libraries, different paradigms, design patterns, and all sorts of elaborate schemes to manage the complexity of code in my various barely-started game projects. I enlisted as a main developer for an online fan game project, and couldn't deliver the goods. I eventually developed some sort of philosophical paralysis about programming in general, questioning my life choices and wondering if I could ever tolerate the career path I was headed towards, until I was snapped out of it from finding Alan Kay, Bret Victor and VPRI on the 'net roughly two years ago. Finally I realised that one of my basic foundations, that of "language being primary / fundamental", was in reality a limiting box of artificial creation :slightly_smiling_face:
And now I really, really want to explore bootstrapping and try to bootstrap a graphical system somehow using shapes instead of source code.

(meanwhile, at work I just do normal frustrating software-engineer stuff :neutral_face: but I will not stay there forever.)

Hi! I'm Spencer. I live in NYC.

I have had crazy ideas about programming languages bouncing around in my head for at least a year now. It seems to me that inadequacies in our programming languages and surrounding tooling are the root cause of most technological troubles.

I've previously worked with computer vision, where I implemented a number of image processing algorithms. The tools we used were grossly insufficient for the task. CUDA was painfully low level, all algorithms became mucked up with performance concerns, code was not portable, build systems were tangled nightmares of dependencies on antiquated software from the 70's... I've been trying to find a better way.

My ideas are still vague and poorly defined but a month ago I started taking these thoughts seriously. I've been learning type theory in an attempt to gain the necessary background to either implement my ideas or determine if they are even feasible. I have a very long way to go to acquire enough background to even understand what I'm getting into... but you have to start somewhere!

Hello everyone! @Nikolas Martens mentioned this slack in his log, so now I'm here. So glad that I found a place with people that share my passion.
Hey @Ivy Reese, glad that you're also here.

My name is Vladimir and I live in Russia, currently in Saint Petersburg.
I always loved programming languages and was curious about alternative ways to program.

Some years ago I became fascinated by Bret Victor's ideas, especially his "Future Programming" and "Seeing Spaces" talks.
This realization that is not technology's fault that we don't have better tools, but just lack of culture, improper attitude -- it felt really striking.
So I wanted to contribute to development of this new culture somehow. Introduce this thinking into daily life.

As a full-time employee I had to work on my projects on weekends.
I would love to do it full time. In order to get that I need to turn project into something commercial.
Something that makes people ready to pay to stop the pain of alternative.

So I tried to create a "Seeing tool" for debugging (not Seeing Space though). A tool that captures trace events for Erlang/OTP platform and visualizes them.
Makes it easier to understand what's happening. Allows to skip the pain of reading hundreds of lines of text logs. It may save hundreds of working hours.
I choosed Erlang/OTP first because underlying model of isolated processes and message passing is really easy to visualize and manipulate with.
Second because it provides powerful tracing API, that makes it very easy to start. And third: I already had experience working in production with Erlang and I loved it.

I took a couple of months break and worked on Batiscaph project: https://github.com/vladimir-vg/batiscaph
Here is the demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VNr7o9eg4Ck

I got a working prototype, yet it's far from being useful in production.
I realized that road to commercializing this project is really long, may take years.
I stopped this project for now and thinking about shorter ways of bringing new thinking into daily life.

Currently I'm thinking about new medium for software and hypermedia (That's why I was reading @Nikolas Martens zells logs: https://github.com/zells/project/tree/master/log).
Got one exciting idea about it. Also it might be easily connected to something not programming related, something that people use in daily life, thus bigger market and maybe easier commercialization.

Hey @Gregg Tavares, I’ve just read your “Life Goals 2018” blog post. Two paragraphs in, I was hooked. I worked at Apple seven years, quit two years ago, and I can relate to everything you write. I’m also in a finding phase, living off my Apple savings, still with enough runway so I’m exactly in that position where it’s comfortable enough to explore whatever, and not uncomfortable enough to get your ass kicked into action. On good days I’m trying to push some projects forward that I consider meaningful, on other days I’m in that “the planet’s going to shit” mood (climate change, politics, etc.) that’s not helping with anything.

Then you write about cancer. Over the last few months, I’ve been spending many hours talking with a good friend once a week during his chemotherapy. We used to work at Apple together, so we talk about the company, technology in general, and the future — stuff we love talking about. Last week they told him they have to stop the chemotherapy, because his body is so weak that it would kill him before the cancer does. I feel like that’s life giving me the (index) finger so I pay attention, because life can give you the (middle) finger anytime.

You live in Japan? Well, where are we going to eat? I’m coming to Tokyo next Wednesday, staying for 10 days in Roppongi. Let’s meet for coffee or food!

Hi Steve, hi everyone. I've been following many of you on Twitter for a good while now, and decided it was time to join the Slack group after @Nikolas Martens mentioned it positively in his most recent Zells project log.

I've lived my entire life in central Alberta, Canada — currently building a house in a remote forest with no phone service and barely any internet.

Life Story (Abridged): I taught myself 3D animation as a kid/teen, which led to a job with a small company in a nearby town that makes some very neat interactive learning media. Over the past decade, I've taught myself to code, and am now the main software dev at the company.

Currently, I'm working on a new suite of tools for our simulation-crafting artists. I want to give them a programming experience that's worthy of being called "Victor-esq", vaguely in the tradition of HyperCard and SmallTalk, loosely inspired by system-centric video games like Factorio or SimCity, with tools as rich and powerful as I'm used to from 3D animation. I'll be sharing progress after I've finished the divergent prototyping phase and start to converge on a specific approach.

I'm also a huge experimental music nerd, so DM me if you want to talk about Max/MSP or Brian Current's "Slanted Time" or Godfried-Willem Raes.

Hi, I’m Brian. I’m a grad student working on Sketch-n-Sketch, a bimodal program editor that allows the programmer to edit their plain-text code or to directly manipulate the program’s output and thereby trigger appropriate program updates. Our main target domain is programs that draw SVGs, because for manipulating graphical shapes there’s already a kind of “standard” mouse UI—think Inkscape or PowerPoint or Illustrator—and a first goal was to imitate the basic interactions of such a regular vector graphics editor, although using plain-text code as the underlying representation of the drawing rather than some hidden graphics-specific internal data structure. More broadly the goal is to figure out reasonable ways to back-propagate manipulations on the output into code transformations, and even more broadly the theme is exploring ways to add more direct manipulation interactions to the programming workflow (e.g. mouse manipulations on code as well as on output). Many of the techniques are not specific to SVG and we are looking at alternative domains. (5min demo vid: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M3P7z1o1ULY Website: https://ravichugh.github.io/sketch-n-sketch/) Thanks for reading!
author: Brian Hempel
text: Hi, I’m Brian. I’m a grad student working on Sketch-n-Sketch, a bimodal program editor that allows the programmer to edit their plain-text code or to directly manipulate the program’s output and thereby trigger appropriate program updates. Our main target domain is programs that draw SVGs, because for manipulating graphical shapes there’s already a kind of “standard” mouse UI—think Inkscape or PowerPoint or Illustrator—and a first goal was to imitate the basic interactions of such a regular vector graphics editor, although using plain-text code as the underlying representation of the drawing rather than some hidden graphics-specific internal data structure. More broadly the goal is to figure out reasonable ways to back-propagate manipulations on the output into code transformations, and even more broadly the theme is exploring ways to add more direct manipulation interactions to the programming workflow (e.g. mouse manipulations on code as well as on output). Many of the techniques are not specific to SVG and we are looking at alternative domains. (5min demo vid: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M3P7z1o1ULY Website: https://ravichugh.github.io/sketch-n-sketch/) Thanks for reading!
